contentBlocks.text: You've learned margin of error. Today: one of the most important cautions in all of statistics!

Correlation means two variables tend to change together, while causation means one variable actually causes the change in the other — correlation alone never proves causation, since a third, unmeasured factor might explain both. Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are strongly correlated (both rise in summer), but ice cream doesn't cause drowning — the real explanation is a third factor: hot weather leads to both more ice cream sales AND more swimming. Explain why it would be a mistake to conclude ice cream causes drowning just from this correlation.
You just learned why correlation doesn't prove causation! Tomorrow we'll apply everything to a real survey scenario.

objectives: Explain the ice-cream-and-drowning example using a third, unmeasured factor
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's population/sample and margin-of-error work.
2. Introduce correlation vs. causation using the ice-cream/drowning example.
3. Have the child explain the third-factor reasoning.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's real-world application.
differentiationTips: Struggling: ask the child what season both ice cream sales AND drownings go up in, to help them spot the hidden third factor (hot weather) themselves
Ready for more: ask the child to come up with their own example of two things that are correlated but where one doesn't cause the other
This is one of the single most important statistical-literacy skills a student can learn — worth real emphasis, since this mistake appears constantly in real media reporting
teacherGuide.answerKey: It would be a mistake because the real explanation is a third factor — hot weather — that independently causes both more ice cream sales and more swimming (and therefore more drowning risk); ice cream sales and drownings rise together not because one causes the other, but because both are driven by the same underlying cause.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Statistics standard S-IC.6: evaluating reports based on data, continuing this week's thread with a genuinely critical statistical-literacy skill.

generationData.instructions: Answer each question about correlation vs. causation.

Why is it a mistake to conclude ice cream causes drowning from the correlation?
